messages.author: 6e0bce06355e4e6c
messages.subject: Combining information
parts:
Dear STAN-users,

Suppose I have 3 dummy variables, indicating whether a survey respondent living in area i smokes, drinks, and exercises. To estimate the (within-area) joint distribution of these variables, I model the survey data as:

n[i,1:K] ~ dmulti( phi[i,1:K] , N[i] )
phi[i,1:K] ~ dirichlet( [1,..,1] )   or:   phi[i,1:K] ~ logisticNormal( [mu[],sigma[] )

where 1:K represents the 2^3 combinations of the dummy variables. Because the survey data is relatively sparse, I want to combine the estimation of phi with additional information about the marginal distribution of each risk factor. Suppose I can model the marginal distribution of each risk factor as:

logit( prob_smoking[i] ) <- inprod( b1[],X1[i,] )
logit( prob_drinking[i] ) <- inprod( b2[],X2[i,] )
logit( prob_exercising[i] ) <- inprod( b3[],X3[i,] ) ,

does it make sense (and is it possible?) to combine the two sources of information, e.g. by specifying something like this in STAN:
 
sum( phi[i,1:K] .* [0 0 0 0 1 1 1 1] ) <- inv_logit( b1*X1) )
sum( phi[i,1:K] .* [0 0 1 1 0 0 1 1] ) <- inv_logit( b2*X2) )
sum( phi[i,1:K] .* [0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1] ) <- inv_logit( b3*X3) )

where the sum of the elements of phi is equal to the prob_smoking, prob_drinking, and prob_exercising?

Thanks!
Marcel

messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Combining information
parts:
I do not really understand the question here.  But as we have always put, what Stan does is to specify the log of the posterior density function of continuous parameters and use NUTS (a variant of HMC) to draw samples from the posterior.  However, how to specify the posterior and make sure the correctness are totally up to the user.  So if you can express your idea of combing information into a posterior distribution, Stan can help.  Then the real question is whether you can write down the posterior mathematically.

--
Jiqiang

messages.author: 6e0bce06355e4e6c
messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] Combining information
parts:
Hi Jiqiang,

Thank you for taking a look and perhaps I can change my question a bit.. Is it somehow possible to define something like: "beta[1] + beta[2] <- inv_logit( 0.01 + theta );" in the model below? I can assign a distribution to beta[1] + beta[2] .. but instead want to use a prediction.


transformed data {
  int alpha[4];
  vector[4] ones;
  for (n in 1:4){
   alpha[n] <- 25;
   ones[n] <- 1;
 } }
parameters{
  simplex[4] beta;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
}
transformed parameters{
  real<lower=0,upper=1> p;
  p <- beta[1] + beta[2];
}
model{
  alpha ~ multinomial(beta);
  beta ~ dirichlet(ones);

  // works:
  // p ~ beta(170,100);
  // doesn't work:
  p <- inv_logit(0.01+ theta );
  theta ~ beta(170,100);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Combining information
parts:
On 8/5/13 9:06 AM, M.F. Jonker wrote:
> Hi Jiqiang,
>
> Thank you for taking a look and perhaps I can change my question a bit.. Is it somehow possible to define something
> like: "beta[1] + beta[2] <- inv_logit( 0.01 + theta );" in the model below? I can assign a distribution to beta[1] +
> beta[2] .. but instead want to use a prediction.

You can't have two parameters with a deterministic link like the
above entails:

beta[1] <- inv_logit(0.01 + theta) - beta[2]

All variables require full support on their declared constraints,
and beta is declared as simplex[4], which means it should have support
on any 4-simplex.

So given your use of

beta ~ dirichlet(ones);

presumably what you want is a uniform distribution on the simplex
beta subject to the above constraint.

In general, all you have to do is define the distribution you want.

I don't know how to do that analytically here, but it's easy enough
with Stan constraints. You can reparameterize in terms of ratios

beta12_frac = beta1 / (beta1 + beta2)

and

beta3_frac = beta3 / (beta3 + beta4).

Given that you know beta1 + beta2, the rest is just algebra.

parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> beta12_ratio;
real<lower=0,upper=1> beta34_ratio;
}
transformed parameters {
simplex[4] beta;
{
real alpha;
real c_alpha;
beta1_p_beta2 <- inv_logit(0.01 + theta);
beta3_p_beta4 <- 1 - alpha;

beta[1] <- beta1_p_beta2 * beta12_ratio;
beta[2] <- beta1_p_beta2 - beta1;
beta[3] <- beta3_p_beta4 * beta34_ratio;
beta[4] <- beta3_p_beta4 - beta3;
}
}

The constraint on the ratios implies a uniform distribution on them and hence
a distribution on the 4-simplex subject to the constraint. (Someone else
should check my work here --- I'm just doing these things for practice
in the hopes of some day getting half as good at this as Ben and Jiqiang are.)

It might just be easier to work on the logit scale for beta
directly and define beta using softmax.

- Bob

> vector[4] ones;
> for (n in 1:4){
> alpha[n] <- 25;
> ones[n] <- 1;
> } }

> real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
> }

> alpha ~ multinomial(beta);

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Combining information
parts:
As Jiqiang points out, this is more of a stats question than
a Stan question. I didn't understand the R notation.

Might it make sense in this case to define three boolean variables for smoking,
drinking and exercising, say y[1], y[2] and y[3] and then model y jointly in
a multivariate regression? The simplest thing to do would be the logistic
version of:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seemingly_unrelated_regressions

where you have separate regressions for the expectation of each variable, but
the errors are tied in a multivariate structure to allow correlations.

I don't actually know if anybody uses this. Is there a section in Andrew
and Jennifer's book on multiple output regression like this? (I don't recall
one.)

- Bob

messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] Combining information

Hi Bob,

Thank you very much! The intended model was something like:

// K = 8
for (s in 1:2)
 for (i in 1:200)
  for (x in 1:8){
    n[s,i,x,1:K] ~ dmultinomial( phi[s,i,x,1:K] )  ;  // joint distribution
    phi[s,i,x,1:K] ~ dirichlet(1,..,1) ;

    // additional structure on marginal distributions
    sum(  phi[s,i,x,1] , phi[s,i,x,2] , phi[s,i,x,3] , phi[s,i,x,4]  )  <-  inv_logit ( b0_r1[s] + inprod( var0[s,i,x, ] , var1[s,x, ] )  + a2[s  ,i] ) ;  // smoking
    sum(  phi[s,i,x,1] , phi[s,i,x,2] , phi[s,i,x,5] , phi[s,i,x,6]  ) <- inv_logit ( b0_r2[s] + inprod( var0[s,i,x, ] , var2[s,x, ] )   + a2[s+2,i] ) ; // drinking
    sum(  phi[s,i,x,1] , phi[s,i,x,3] , phi[s,i,x,5] , phi[s,i,x,7] )  <- inv_logit ( b0_r3[s] + inprod( var0[s,i,x, ] , var3[s,x, ] ) + a2[s+4,i] ) ; //exercising
  }
 
a2 ~ MVCAR ;

But you're right, if <- can't be used, another model is more appropriate. I'll have a look at the SUR!

Marcel

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Combining information
parts:
Hi Marcel, STAN-users,

Just a comment from a different perspective:

Marcel, I was just wondering whether you considered modeling the logit-probabilities of each of the three binary dummies with a trivariate normal distribution. If you then specify a prior for the correlation matrix of the log-odds of the three dummies, you can specify separate priors on the means and variances or marginal variances of the log-odds of each of the three binary dummies. Is this what you are looking for?

Luc
